The USS George Washington is relieving the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East, and the movement of these two massive aircraft carriers is both strategic and symbolic.

   One of the most sensitive stories in this nearly six-month Iran War is the toll it has taken on American servicemembers. Nearly 20 U.S. servicemembers have died in the Middle East since the war began, including in Iranian attacks in Kuwait and Jordan.

   A central component of President Trump’s war strategy is a massive naval blockade of Iran that is meant to choke off the country’s economy. Doing so is logistically quite complicated and requires a large number of U.S. ships across the region. Those ships host thousands of U.S. servicemembers, and Trump has suggested the blockade could be in place for a prolonged time.

   The USS Lincoln has been at the heart of the bombing and pressure campaign against Iran. It spent more than 200 days in a combat zone and launched more than 10,000 sorties, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said.

   There have been reports that this deployment has taken its toll on both the ship and its sailors. Getting fresh food has been challenging at times, and some servicemembers have dealt with mental-health challenges. Senate Democrats are demanding answers from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about the toll the deployment has taken on U.S. forces.

   Trump has dismissed reports that the ship has been at sea too long, and Hegseth said the issues have been “completely misrepresented.”

   In recent months, Iran’s approach has been to mostly delay and stall negotiations, taking a toll on the U.S. military. The White House has bristled at reports that it is running low on munitions , and they are similarly bristling at reports about naval deployments.

   Maintaining logistical supply chains and servicemember morale during extended wars are key to military success, and an indefinite blockade is likely to test the Pentagon’s ability to do both.

When Trump announced last year that he was demolishing part of the White House to make way for a ballroom, he framed it as a matter of aesthetics and space. After the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June, Trump administration officials looked to build support for an agreement they hoped would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and wind down the war. Pentagon Rotates Aircraft Carriers, Showing Toll of the Iran War
 
Plus, Iran’s plan to escalate the conflict with the U.S., and how Trump came to refer to his ballroom as a military project
 
 
U.S. NAVY
 

Good morning. The USS George Washington is relieving the USS Abraham Lincoln in the Middle East, and the movement of these two massive aircraft carriers is both strategic and symbolic.

 

One of the most sensitive stories in this nearly six-month Iran War is the toll it has taken on American servicemembers. Nearly 20 U.S. servicemembers have died in the Middle East since the war began, including in Iranian attacks in Kuwait and Jordan.

 

A central component of President Trump’s war strategy is a massive naval blockade of Iran that is meant to choke off the country’s economy. Doing so is logistically quite complicated and requires a large number of U.S. ships across the region. Those ships host thousands of U.S. servicemembers, and Trump has suggested the blockade could be in place for a prolonged time.

 

The USS Lincoln has been at the heart of the bombing and pressure campaign against Iran. It spent more than 200 days in a combat zone and launched more than 10,000 sorties, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said.

 

There have been reports that this deployment has taken its toll on both the ship and its sailors. Getting fresh food has been challenging at times, and some servicemembers have dealt with mental-health challenges. Senate Democrats are demanding answers from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about the toll the deployment has taken on U.S. forces.

 

Trump has dismissed reports that the ship has been at sea too long, and Hegseth said the issues have been “completely misrepresented.”

 

In recent months, Iran’s approach has been to mostly delay and stall negotiations, taking a toll on the U.S. military. The White House has bristled at reports that it is running low on munitions, and they are similarly bristling at reports about naval deployments.

 

Maintaining logistical supply chains and servicemember morale during extended wars are key to military success, and an indefinite blockade is likely to test the Pentagon’s ability to do both.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

U.S.-South Korea: Joint military exercises between the U.S. and South Korea began as scheduled Monday, after Trump said he would reduce them.

 

Trump’s Monday: The president is expected to receive his intelligence briefing at 11 a.m. ET, and he will participate in a policy meeting later in the day.

What I’m Following

 
 
ANDREW HARNIK/GETTY IMAGES
 

Trump takes a different tack on his ballroom project. When Trump announced last year that he was demolishing part of the White House to make way for a ballroom, he framed it as a matter of aesthetics and space. But as the project has faced legal challenges, Trump has leaned in to arguments of national security.

 

Iran’s leaders had a secret war plan. After the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June, Trump administration officials looked to build support for an agreement they hoped would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and wind down the war. Intercepted communications and other intelligence suggest a strategic shift by Iran’s hard-line leaders to raise the costs for the U.S. and its regional allies.

 

Democrats see signs of hope in typically Republican Iowa. As state fair season takes place in Iowa, Republicans find themselves in an unfamiliar position: trailing Democrats in a top race and facing serious challenges in several others. Some GOP candidates didn’t mention Trump during their highest-profile fair appearances. Democrats, meanwhile, are pouring millions into the state’s races, as rural economic pain from Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran erodes GOP support in some areas.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Trump returned to an old playbook to break a yearslong stalemate with North Korea, ordering cuts to annual military exercises with South Korea.

 

• The Trump administration policy revoking protected status for Haitian workers is causing a labor shortage in Florida.

 

• With Jair Bolsonaro under house arrest, the future of the Brazil’s conservative movement rests with his eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro.
